Leicester City are facing a potentially significant squad overhaul next summer, with nine players expected to leave the club as several contract decisions approach at the King Power Stadium.

The Foxes are focused on securing promotion from League One on the first attempt, but the club’s hierarchy will also need to consider long-term squad planning as the season draws to a close.

According to a report from Leicester Mercury, academy graduate Sammy Braybrooke is among those whose future requires attention, with his current contract due to expire next summer.

The 22-year-old midfielder has become an important member of Russell Martin’s side this season, and Leicester will be keen to avoid losing a promising homegrown talent without receiving a transfer fee.

Braybrooke is not the only academy graduate approaching the end of his current agreement. Goalkeeper Jakub Stolarczyk and defender Ben Nelson are also expected to see their contracts expire next summer, although their respective long-term knee injuries could complicate decisions over their futures.

Meanwhile, Bobby De Cordova-Reid and goalkeeper David Cornell are also approaching the end of their Leicester contracts. The former has registered nine goals in 80 appearances since arriving from Fulham in 2024, but an extension appears unlikely.

The club will additionally need to assess the futures of several loan players, with Tammy Watson, Kamari Doyle, Harry Howell and Christian McFarlane expected to return to their parent clubs when their temporary arrangements conclude.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Further contractual matters remain to be addressed in 2028, with John Lundstram, Will Alves, Harry Souttar, Bade Aluko and Alex McCarthy among those whose agreements are nearing their end.

Leicester’s immediate priority remains promotion, but the club cannot afford to overlook its long-term planning. Finding an agreement with Braybrooke could be particularly important as they look to retain emerging talent.

#1355. Man United hire private jet to get Mauricio Pochettino straight to Manchester after final USA game in Cincinnati - and new boss is expected to start work as soon as he steps off the plane!

Published: 11:27 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:55 EST, 16 November 2026

Manchester United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England in the early hours of Wednesday morning after he finishes work as US national team coach.

Pochettino’s last game in charge is against Haiti in Cincinnati, which kicks off at midnight on Tuesday UK time. The 54-year-old will speak to the media and say farewell to his players before jumping on a plane to Manchester which has been organised by United.

It will enable Pochettino to sleep before he lands in the UK on Wednesday morning ready to go straight to Carrington and start work.

He will be accompanied by first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott.

It has emerged that three other members of his trusted coaching team – assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez and his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino – were allowed to travel to Manchester at the weekend after the US won the first leg against Haiti 6-0 in Miami.

It means that Pochettino’s back-room staff have been able to make a headstart in their preparations for his first game in charge against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. It is a huge fixture in the calendar for United, but even more so because he takes over a team languishing in the relegation zone.

Man United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England after he finishes work as US national team coach

Pochettino will take charge of his final match as USA boss in Cincinnati before boarding the direct flight to Manchester

Pochettino's long-time assistant Jesus Perez is one of three trusted staff members who have already been given permission to travel to Manchester

Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty, and is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference on Friday lunchtime.

Speaking ahead of the second leg against Haiti at the TQL Stadium, Pochettino said: ‘I am with Miguel, Sylvia and Alec and after they are going to join me in Manchester.

‘The next question is where are Jesus, Toni and Sebastiano? They are ahead. After the game (in Miami), they flew to Manchester and they are there in advance. That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the US national team.

‘They are there preparing everything because on Wednesday, when we arrive, it’s going to be non-stop and then we start with playing games.’

#1353. New CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein (blue; artist’s illustration) together with RNA and DNA (orange). A new therapy uses the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to treat a rare genetic disorder called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/SPL

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic condition that can cause episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, a type of hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary-angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send the cells off for gene editing before infusing them back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR–Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two of Intellia’s in vivo trials for a different disorder. The agency did so after a participant with additional health conditions developed signs of liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after extra safety measures were added.

#1352. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

“I’m really happy for Bradley, because you were asking me yesterday about him, not making the numbers,” Iraola smiled. “Also Florian [Wirtz], and I think both of them played really, really well. They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

We can look at the late switch off in due course but the only place to begin is with Barcola, who looked ready for business as early as the eighth minute when his first touch was a cushioned back heel, taking possession by crossing one leg behind the other, and how he seized his moment.

Liverpool had already taken the lead when Ronald Araújo rose powerfully to head in a Kostas Tsimikas corner but, two minutes after, the Barcola show began, a confident right-footed shot being swept past Lukas Jungwirth from 10 yards after some good build-up play from Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Koumas.

Liverpool needed Barcola to deliver as much as the player himself needed to prove a little point and there is absolutely nothing wrong with having a cause to light a fire. Like a batsman who has been waiting nervously to get off the mark, soon the France international began playing his shots.

There were cushioned touches, changes of gear and even a stunned pass to Ryan Gravenberch, using his heel, that showed confidence had started surging through him and how obvious that was when Wirtz sent him scampering away in the 37th minute to finish with his left foot.

A brilliant night should have been glossed by Koumas’s first European goal – he matched Steven Gerrard in becoming just the second player aged 21 and under to assist and score for Liverpool in a Champions League game – but LASK kept pushing and exploited spaces to halve the deficit with a double from Florian Flecker, much to Alisson Becker’s obvious disgust.

A young Liverpool team has been selected to face Linz – the third youngest, according to Opta, that the club have fielded in the Champions League – and Andoni Iraola is being mindful of players such as Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister being overburdened ahead of Saturday’s trip to Brentford.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Asked about Liverpool’s youthful team, Iraola said: “For me Trey [Nyoni], [Lewis] Koumas and Rio [Ngumoha] are young players coming in from the academy but they are first team players.

“They are first team players because we trust them, and in our situation, where we have some injuries, and we come from playing three days ago. I think they can play well, and I hope they do well.”

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

West Ham United are reportedly preparing for a major squad overhaul under Scott Parker, with Taty Castellanos emerging as a leading candidate to leave the London Stadium in the January transfer window.

The Hammers have endured a difficult start to their Championship campaign, and the new manager is already assessing the squad ahead of the upcoming transfer window.

According to a Football Insider report, former West Ham scout Mick Brown believes Castellanos could be among the first players shown the exit door as Parker looks to reshape his squad.

The Argentine striker has struggled to make an impact in the second tier, registering just one goal in 14 league appearances this season. Despite arriving from Lazio with considerable expectations, the 28-year-old has failed to establish himself as a dependable attacking option.

Brown believes the forward does not provide enough quality overall or in front of goal to justify a prominent role in Parker’s plans.

The former scout suggested that several members of the current squad are not delivering the consistency required to secure promotion, making changes necessary when the transfer window reopens.

West Ham have already started identifying potential additions, with strengthening their attacking options emerging as an important priority.

Castellanos could therefore find himself sacrificed as Parker searches for a more reliable centre-forward capable of leading the promotion charge.

Parker has considerable experience of achieving promotion from the Championship, having guided Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley into the Premier League.

The 46-year-old will be determined to replicate that success at his former club, and making the right recruitment decisions in January could prove crucial.

Moving on from Castellanos might be one of the first steps towards building a squad capable of returning to the top flight.

#1350. Calafiori: ‘Best’ moment of my career at Arsenal, Italy a ‘long-term journey’

Riccardo Calafiori admits he’s having the ‘best’ moment of his career at Arsenal, sees the Italy project as a ‘long-term journey’ and confirms he’d like to return to Roma one day.

Italy international Calafiori received an award from Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri on Tuesday. Gualtieri presented the Arsenal defender with a special plaque “for the outstanding results achieved” in 2026, including Arsenal’s Premier League title.

“I want to thank Mayor Gualtieri. I felt quite emotional walking in here today,” Calafiori told reporters via Gazzetta.

“Thank you for this recognition, which fills me with pride. I always try to represent my Roman roots abroad. Whenever I come back, it’s always a great emotion.”

Talking about his spell at Arsenal, the Italian defender added: “I think it’s the best moment of my career. I feel like a leader in the dressing room, and I try to help my teammates and the younger players.”

Born in Rome and a product of the Roma academy, Calafiori already said in the past that he’d like to play for the Giallorossi again one day.

During today’s award ceremony, he confirmed: “I hope to win as much as possible over the coming years. Then, in the more distant future, as I’ve always said, I would love to return to Roma.”

Calafiori received a special plaque, but he also had a gift for Rome’s Mayor: a signed Arsenal away jersey.

“I spoke with the Mayor about the new stadium project, and I can’t wait to see it completed,” the defender said.

Calafiori was also asked his thoughts on Roma’s results this season: “Everyone speaks highly of Gasperini and his ability to get the best out of players. I hope he can achieve the best possible results by the end of the season,” he replied.

Calafiori started Italy’s last two games against France and Belgium, securing a 3-1 win against Les Bleus, but also suffering a 4-1 loss away in Belgium.

“We are sorry about the elimination from the Nations League, but there’s a desire to start again from certain principles. It’s a long-term journey,” he concluded.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

THIS is the equivalent of a “participation medal” that children these days expect and think they’re world-beaters…

1 title with Arsenal and you get a special prize? LMAO

#1349. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

PSG have made a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign, their worst since Luis Enrique’s first season in charge. Starting with two draws and a defeat, they have rallied with three successive victories to climb up to sixth as the head coach, as he tends to do in the league, rotates his midfielders and forwards like crazy, to whose ranks he has added the World Cup-winner Ferran Torres. The summer signing scored a hat-trick in his Champions League debut for the club, a 6-1 mauling of Slovan Bratislava.

City, too, started their European campaign with a win, Erling Haaland scoring both goals in the 2-0 victory over Porto at the Dragao and you won’t need me to remind you that they have won all six of their Premier League games to lead Arsenal by three points at the top of the table.

Aston Villa could face a major squad reshuffle next summer, with six players potentially heading towards the exit door as Unai Emery and the club’s hierarchy assess their long-term futures at Villa Park.

The Midlands club have several important contractual decisions to make, with the futures of experienced first-team players and squad members requiring attention ahead of the next transfer window.

According to a report from Birmingham Live, Emiliano Buendia, Ross Barkley, Tyrone Mings, Marco Bizot, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho could be among those whose futures need resolving.

Buendia is arguably the most interesting case. The Argentine playmaker has worked his way back into Emery’s plans after a difficult spell and has demonstrated his attacking quality since returning from Bayer Leverkusen. However, with his contract approaching its expiry, Villa need to reach an agreement if they want to avoid losing him.

Barkley is another player whose situation deserves attention. The experienced midfielder has provided useful depth, but Villa must consider whether retaining him fits their plans for the coming seasons.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Mings and Wan-Bissaka also face an uncertain future, with the defensive department potentially undergoing further changes. Although both bring valuable experience, Emery will need to assess whether they remain essential to his long-term project.

Goalkeeper Bizot is another name to watch. The Dutchman has served as a dependable alternative between the posts, but his position could become difficult to maintain if Villa decide to reshape their goalkeeping options.

Garnacho is yet to start a match for Aston Villa, and a permanent move will depend on certain conditions being met.

Villa must carefully evaluate their options before making final decisions. Allowing several experienced players to depart could create opportunities to refresh the squad, although Emery will be keen to preserve sufficient depth for domestic and European commitments.

Published: 06:21 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EST, 16 November 2026

Lamine Yamal mercilessly taunted England rival Elliot Anderson as tensions flared during the Three Lions’ spectacular victory over Spain on Sunday night.

England held on for a memorable 3-2 victory in Madrid after Anderson was given his marching orders with just under 30 minutes remaining.

Thomas Tuchel’s side were three goals in front and cruising when Anderson - looking to atone for a sloppy error from Jarrel Quansah - cynically hauled down 19-year-old Yamal as he barrelled down on goal.

Spain were awarded a penalty for the infringement, and Anderson was sent off - much to the Manchester City star’s bemusement.

But Yamal, aggrieved by Anderson’s challenge, made a beeline for the midfielder following the challenge. According to Spanish reports, the attacker mouthed ‘tonto, tonto’ to his rival following his dismissal.

The colloquial term can mean a number of things, varying from idiot, fool or stupid, but in any case is far from a term of affection.

Lamine Yamal was spotted taunting Elliot Anderson after the Manchester City midfielder was sent off for a challenge on the winger

The moment came in England's historic 3-2 win over the World Champions

Anderson blanked the 19-year-old while a VAR review confirmed the on-field official’s decision was the right one, eventually trudging off the pitch.

A fired-up Yamal galvanised the reigning world champions as they searched for an unlikely comeback.

Mikel Oyarzabal, the man who scored Spain’s winner against England two years ago in the 2024 Euros final, converted the spot kick before Nico Williams scored Spain’s second after latching on to an excellent Yamal cross.

However, Las Rojas fell short, with Sunday’s defeat their first in an imperious 43-game run.

A jubilant Thomas Tuchel hailed the match as his ‘best performance of my time as manager’.

‘What a performance we put out there for 60 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up,’ Tuchel said after the game. ’Thirty minutes against Spain with ten men feels like three hours.

‘It was a statement victory. It was on the highest level football-wise. It is a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.’

#1346. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1345. Calafiori honoured in Rome for his achievements at Arsenal and beyond

Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri honoured Italy defender Riccardo Calafiori today for his title victory with Arsenal and for being an ‘ambassador for our city around the world.’

Italy international Calafiori received a special plaque in his hometown of Rome today, not just for his Premier League title win with Arsenal in the 2025-26 season.

“It’s a great pleasure to welcome and greet Riccardo Calafiori,” Rome Mayor Gualtieri said (via Gazzetta) during the award ceremony

“He is an extraordinary sportsman whose achievements make us proud. He is an ambassador for our city around the world, standing out not only for winning the Premier League but also for his style and elegance. He is a wonderful person. That makes us proud: he flies the flag for Rome in the United Kingdom and around the world.”

Calafiori held a press conference after receiving the award, saying that this is the best moment of his career and confirming he’d like to return to Roma one day, in a “more distant future.”

Calafiori was born in Rome and came up through the Roma academy.

The ex-Bologna defender made his senior Roma debut in 2020 under Paulo Fonseca.

He made ten senior appearances with the Giallorossi before joining Genoa on loan in January 2022, then Basel on a permanent deal the following summer.

After two seasons with the Swiss club, he returned to Serie A, signing for Bologna, where he spent one season and helped the Rossoblu qualify for the Champions League.

In the summer of 2024, after featuring for Italy at the Euros, he joined Arsenal for circa €50m.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1344. Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an important step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, says geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The new framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology company that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

With the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, says a new report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Nature Mental Health editorial | 6 min read

Get the gist in the accompanying policy brief (9 min read)

Reference: Nature Mental Health Earth–Brain–Health Commission report

The lawless simulated world of blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) — which is just about to release its sixth iteration — offers researchers an intricately crafted testbed for road-safety experiments, says computer scientist Julius Schöning. (BBC | 7 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was announced as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, says Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

Let me know what other science-fiction books I should add to the pile, along with your feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

#1343. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1342. Newspaper names Spalletti’s favourite January target for Juventus’ attack

Tuttosport reports that Alexander Sorloth remains Luciano Spalletti’s favourite attacking target, but Juventus would only welcome the Atletico Madrid forward on loan with an option to buy.

Juventus are expected to be busy in the January transfer window, as the Serie A giants will look for a new central midfielder, a left-back, and a centre-forward.

It is no secret that the Bianconeri will have limited financial resources for the winter transfer window, forcing the club to focus on targets potentially available at a low price.

This is not believed to be the case for Folarin Balogun, who is no longer part of Monaco’s plans but was close to joining Everton for €50m last summer, a fee the Old Lady can’t afford.

Gianluca Scamacca of Atalanta is also being monitored by the Bianconeri, but according to Tuttosport, Atletico Madrid’s Alexander Sorloth remains Spalletti’s top target.

Juventus already held talks with Atletico and Sorloth last summer, when Spalletti even spoke directly with the Norwegian international.

Ironically, Sorloth is getting less game time than last season because of Juventus loanee Jonathan David, so he is considering leaving the Wanda Metropolitano in January.

According to Tuttosport, Spalletti favours Sorloth for his eye for goal and physicality. Spalletti wants a classic centre-forward, as Randal Kolo Muani and Nick Woltemade aren’t entirely suited to his style.

Tuttosport, however, warns that Juventus would only consider signing Sorloth on loan with an option to buy, as they are unwilling to commit to a future permanent transfer for a player who will turn 31 in December.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1341. The boyish, Lego-obsessed son of a farmer who quit Man City to become England's No 1: How James Trafford - with £95m spent on him - is maturing to star for Leeds and the Three Lions

Published: 14:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:35 EST, 16 November 2026

'It was like meeting a kid at a sixth-form careers day'. That was the verdict, slightly unflattering but endearing all the same, of one Premier League chief after encountering James Trafford.

When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.

He is the son of a Cumbrian farmer and the Lego was of a tractor, which he would save for later in the tournament. 'You don't want to go too early,' he said.

None of this is a criticism. Far from it. There was a boyish charm, an innocence, even, and Trafford was engaging company. Nonetheless, he did not sound ready for the likes of a World Cup semi-final against Argentina. Thomas Tuchel agreed.

But every boy will one day become a man. On a ferocious and febrile night in Madrid, no place for adolescents, we may just have witnessed James Trafford's graduation ceremony.

Without his double save in stoppage-time, England would have left Spain without a famous, and deserved, victory. One Spanish title labelled it 'la actuacion de su vida', the performance of his life. You wonder how much they saw of his loan spell at Accrington Stanley, but the sentiment stands.

James Trafford celebrates with Jarell Quansah, Dan Burn and Ezri Konsa during his starring performance in Spain

Trafford pictured with his farmer father, David, in the cab of his tractor with their dogs (Source: James Trafford)

Madrid daily AS exclaimed: 'Magisterio de Trafford!' Translated, 'A Trafford Masterclass!'. They claim he was the reason Spain could not complete their comeback, and they would be right.

When Tuchel stood with us in a corridor of the Metropolitano Stadium on the eve of the game, he had no issue confirming that Trafford would start. His message, though, was clear - it was sink or swim for a goalkeeper who turned 24 last month.

Not only did Trafford keep his head above water, it was he who pulled the team ashore. It was he to whom his senior colleagues ran in celebration. Ezri Konsa nearly took the shirt off Trafford's back, such was the force of his gratitude. But maybe this was the occasion when Trafford took the No 1 jersey from the back of Jordan Pickford, the holder for nearly a decade.

Pickford has done nothing wrong. Were Trafford to still display that maturity deficit, Pickford would be a reliable custodian heading to Euro 2028. This is not Peter Shilton post Italia 90, an uncomfortable truth of a great in need of the retirement barn. The 32-year-old has plenty to give on the back of all he has already given.

This, admitted Tuchel after the 3-2 win, is a selection dilemma that allows a manager to sleep well at night.

'There is no headache at all!' he boomed. 'I'm so far away from a headache, I cannot imagine.

Trafford left Manchester City with the plan to usurp Jordan Pickford as England No 1

Jude Bellingham certainly seemed impressed with the performance of the goalkeeper

'This is what we wanted. This is the best thing that can happen to all of us, also to Pickers. It is amazing how they push each other, and if then Traff has a performance like this, he has it because he knows he's well prepared. He gets the push from his colleagues and competitors.'

Tuchel has seen enough of Trafford in training and around camp to believe he is ready for promotion. He has watched him for Leeds, where he rates as the best performing goalkeeper in the Premier League. His 'net goals prevented' (4.4) and 'save percentage' (81.4) are higher than any rival this season, including Pickford.

'You always have to deserve your place,' added Tuchel. 'You will never get a gift and just get a game (for the sake of it). So he deserved to play and we expected this kind of performance. It was not only the last save, but also the build-up play and not losing focus. He has proved it on this stage, so this gives him a lot of belief. Now, it's on him to keep going for it.'

It, you presume, is the No 1 jersey. Trafford has made no secret of his desire to take it from Pickford, and he told us in the summer that such ambition was the motivation behind him wanting to leave Manchester City for a second time.

That day, he flipped his room key with a magician's sleight of hand throughout the interview, a dexterity useful for Lego. Better still for fingertip saves such as the one to deny Aymeric Laporte in the 91st minute.

Also in the gift pack from his girlfriend were two face masks. 'Very thoughtful,' he quipped. But that is another observation, bordering on concern, that some prospective buyers have made in recent years - on the goalkeeping scale of uber professional to joker, he resides too close to the latter. We have seen, even this season, the odd concentration lapse that speaks to that thought.

Trafford has played a starring role in goal since moving to Leeds United in the summer

But there was also a feeling that Trafford needed more exposure and responsibility before the penny dropped and his value was realised. Already, £95million has been spent on him in transfer fees.

At Leeds, and now with England, he has been given that stage, as Tuchel calls it. The head coach maintains that Pickford is his first choice, but it was Trafford he picked for both Nations League fixtures against Spain, the ones that really mattered, the ones that would strengthen or threaten his own employment.

As for Trafford's career prospects, to revisit our opening line, England's No 1 sounds like a fair vocation.

Thomas Tuchel wants England to use victory in the Nations League finals as a springboard to winning Euro 2028 at Wembley.

The head coach admits it has taken him a while to recover from the trauma of his side’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July, for which he was heavily criticised.

But after beating world champions Spain 3-2 on Sunday night, topping their Nations League group ahead of March’s quarter-finals and next summer's finals, Tuchel is finally able to look forward with positivity and belief.

‘I saw the celebrations in Portugal when they won the Nations League,’ he said. ‘It’s just the best, the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves and to gain confidence, to see where we are and to adjust our game where we need to, that’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it.’

England have won five of their six matches since the World Cup, losing only to Spain at Wembley in September. In the build up to that game, Tuchel was involved in heated exchanges with observers who continued to question his tactics in the final half hour against Argentina.

’It took me a while to digest (the World Cup exit) and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together,’ he said.

‘We had reviews and so on, but clarity then came together with the players. Straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps. The ideas became more clear for me, even if it was not so easy the first week, to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together.

‘(Spain) was a complete performance that makes me very proud. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up in this moment.’

Tuchel, though, has rejected the idea that seeing out the win Madrid was proof that he has learned from his mistakes in Atlanta

‘Not at all, I think we would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11,’ he said. ‘For me, it was Mexico reloaded (not Argentina). It's one man down, but what can you do? It is their strength to have ball possession, to overload and find the gaps. It just plays totally into their hands and it comes wave after wave. It felt like three hours and thirty minutes!’

#1340. Pochettino's Transfer Solution: Man Utd Academy Star Harry Amass

Mauricio Pochettino is the new manager of Manchester United, and he already knows that he has some major issues to solve within his squad.

The Argentine has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to leave the USMNT after their Nations League quarter-final second-leg clash with Haiti and make the switch to Old Trafford, where his first game will come on Sunday afternoon when they travel to Anfield to face off against arch-rivals Liverpool.

The boss will only have a number of days to assess his squad before picking his first starting lineup, but there are areas of the squad that are already short of quality and options, and the club will be looking to address that in the January transfer window.

In the summer the club were looking to add a forward and a left-back to the squad, but after spending £155m on Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Carlos Baleba, the club opted against bringing in any further additions.

Benjamin Sesko has since been ruled out for several months with a recurrence of his shin injury, meaning the striker position is short on quality, while at left-back both Luke Shaw and Patrick Dorgu have been dealing with injury issues throughout the campaign.

But while the striker situation has got the depth across the attack to survive for a few more weeks before any deals can be done, the left-back position is not so lucky, and Pochettino must start to look at options to solve the problem between now and then.

The 54-year-old has never been shy of giving young players an opportunity in the first team. It was he who gave Luke Shaw his debut at Southampton as a 17-year-old, while he also gave players like Dele Alli, Philippe Coutinho, Harrison Reed, Kyle Walker-Peters, Xavi Simons, and Harry Kane their big breaks at the top level.

Now at Old Trafford, where he has the chance to revolutionise Man Utd, he will have the responsiblity of ensuring that the famous pathway from Carrington to the first-team doesn't disappear.

The academy at Man Utd has been legendary in the Premier League era, producing top stars like Ryan Giggs, David Beckham, Paul Scholes, Marcus Rashford, and Paul Pogba. The biggest talent now is JJ Gabriel, although the 16-year-old is set to depart the club for Real Madrid after a fallout between the club and his family over his involvement in first-team games.

But there is another youngster who is ready to make an impact in the first-team, and Pochettino could solve a major issue by giving him his chance.

Youngster Harry Amass has been one of the most impressive young players to come out of the academy system at Man Utd in recent years, but he has found opportunities in the first-team hard to come by so far.

The 19-year-old spent last season out on loan at Sheffield Wednesday before joining Norwich in January, where he suffered a season-ending injury after just a handful of appearances.

But he returned to Old Trafford in the summer and was part of the pre-season squad, even scoring in the win over Rosenborg. Despite the injuries suffered by Shaw and Dorgu, however, Carrick still handed him just 18 minutes of action before he was sacked, preferring to use Diogo Dalot, Noussair Mazraoui and Ayden Heaven out of position instead.

Pochettino will see a lot of what he saw in Shaw at Southampton in Amass. He is quick, powerful, excellent on the ball, and good defensively. In one-on-one situations, he can hold his own too, and while he looks small, he is almost 6ft tall.

Whenever he has been given a chance to shine he has taken it, too. So much so, that former teammate Charlie McNeill described him as 'ridiculous'.

“He’s a joke, honestly. He’s so good, on the ball he’s ridiculous and he’s not shy of putting a tackle in. He's good enough to have a future there [Man Utd."

Pochettino has a chance to give him his opportunity and figure out whether a big signing is really needed in January, or if the club have enough to get by until the summer when Shaw will likely leave, and a new first-choice arrival can join to compete with Amass and Dorgu.

#1339. I Was 'Incredible' At Celtic, Now I Own a Bar in Thailand Frequented by Henrik Larsson and Tyson Fury

Scottish football has been dominated by two teams since 1986, with only Celtic and Rangers winning the league titles in the last 40 years.

Celtic have been the more dominant of the great Glasgow rivals, winning 22 titles compared to Rangers' 18 in that time, although the green side of the city has the benefit of being in the division the entire time, while Rangers spent four years climbing back into the top flight following administration and liquidation in 2012, which saw them restart in the fourth tier.

Celtic, meanwhile, have been able to build a number of dominant sides over the years, including during the period of 2000 and 2006, where they won four league titles.

That squad, managed by Martin O'Neill and then Gordon Strachan, was stacked with some incredible talent. The likes of Henrik Larsson, John Hartson, Alan Thompson, Chris Sutton, Bobo Balde, Stillian Petrov were all key members of the squad, and all wrote themselves into Celtic folklore in that period.

But someone who is often overlooked is winger Didier Agathe, who made 122 appearances for the club after joining in a deal worth just £27,000 from Hibernian.

Once described as 'incredible' by Sutton after playing alongside him, the Frenchman was one of the quickest players in Celtic's history, and is fondly remembered for his time at Parkhead.

But these days, the 51-year-old lives an incredibly different life as a bar owner in Thailand.

According to Eddie Murphy, the owner of 'The Irish House' in Pattaya, Agathe is now a part-owner of the Celtic-themed bar.

Murphy opened the bar in Thailand last year, and revealed to Glasgow Live that they have had some very familiar faces visit, including Hoops legend Henrik Larsson.

“I'd had the bar for around a year, before he wanted to buy into the bar and improve it.

“We've had Tyson Fury and Henrik Larsson in it, and when Didier Agathe came in, he loved it and he wanted to buy it. When he came, he phoned (Lubomir) Moravcik and said, 'You need to see this bar, it's unbelievable'.

According to Murphy, the bar is the only Celtic-themed bar of its kind in Thailand, and offers tourists a taste of home by offering traditional pub food and Guinness.

Agathe is someone who is fondly remembered in Glasgow for his role in their success during his six seasons with the club, and it's clear that he has taken that affection for the club with him into his post-football career choices.

Now based in Thailand, the ex-winger owns 50% of the bar and is constantly in contact with Mr. Murphy in order to help run the business and improve it.

While he only scored 11 goals in his 122 appearances, it was his pace and direct running that often caught the eye, and helped the team transition from defence to attack very quickly.

Signed after a brief stint at Hibernian, Agathe went on to become a regular under O'Neill at Celtic where he won three Scottish Premiership titles, three Scottish Cups, a Scottish League Cup, and also reached the UEFA Cup final in 2003, where the Bhoys were beaten by Jose Mourinho's Porto side.

Celtic signed the 'next Henrikh Larsson' back in 2011, but the player left the Scottish club without a goal and ultimately retired at 29.

#1338. How much Inter paid for Spence, Tottenham pocket €30.75m plus bonus

The financial details behind Inter’s deal with Tottenham Hotspur for Djed Spence have been revealed, with the cost reaching €30.75m plus a series of add-ons.

The 26-year-old made the move from Spurs to Inter in mid-August, after an excellent performance for England at the 2026 World Cup.

He was their second choice for the role of right wing-back, after being out-bid by Chelsea for Marco Palestra, and will eventually cost around half that fee.

Calcio e Finanza looked through the Inter accounts and found the precise details of the agreement to buy Spence from Tottenham Hotspur.

The basic fee is worth €30.75m split into three instalments in the summer of 2026, 2027 and 2028 of €10.25m each.

There are also potential add-ons worth up to a total of €5.125m tied to various achievements for the club and the player.

This is €512,500 for each Serie A title won by Inter, as long as Spence played at least 50 per cent of those matches, but can only be used at most twice for a total of €1.025m.

In order for it to count, Spence must’ve played a minimum of 45 minutes per match.

The same fee and system are used for reaching the Champions League semi-final, again playing 50 per cent of games, and at most in two seasons for a maximum of €1.025m.

Simply qualifying for the Champions League is worth €512,500 when playing 50 per cent of Serie A matches, but this bonus can be activated up to three times for a peak of €1.5375m.

Winning the Champions League is a one-off bonus worth €1.025m, again with Spence participating in half those games.

If the player reaches 30 goal contributions (between goals and assists) in all competitive games, there is another bonus going to Tottenham of €512,500.

This is not necessarily in one season, but once the target is reached, it cannot be repeated.

If all these bonuses are activated, Spence will have cost €35,875m.

That is not all, because Tottenham also have a percentage of his future sale fee worth 10.25 per cent of the total, but it also applies in case of a loan with option to buy.

If Spence is released as part of an exchange of players, then Inter must give Spurs 10.25 per cent of the calculated value.

#1337. He Wore Southampton's Number 7 Shirt After Le Tissier - Then He Was Given 2-Year Prison Sentence

Southampton are currently aiming to win promotion back to the Premier League this season under Tonda Eckert following the Spygate scandal last term, and it was a similar story in the 2005-06 campaign.

After an absolute mess of a 2004-05 season, Southampton were relegated to England's second tier after spending the previous 27 years in the top flight.

The great work done by the likes of Matthew Le Tissier in keeping the club in the Premier League was undone, and it was up to Harry Redknapp to secure an immediate return the following season having failed to save the club from the drop.

As ever when a club suffers relegation, there were huge changes to the playing squad at St Mary's, with the likes of Peter Crouch, Kevin Phillips and Fabrice Fernandes departing, and those three were among 24 departures during the whole campaign.

With so many outgoings, it was clear that there would be a lot of incomings too, especially with Redknapp at the helm, and 15 players arrived at St Mary's to boost their promotion push.

Saints barely spent any money either as they counted the cost of relegation, with Ricardo Fuller joining from arch-rivals Portsmouth for a bargain £90,000.

On the same day, the south coast outfit also completed the signing of experienced Polish centre-back Tomasz Hajto, who moved to England after spells in Germany with MSV Duisburg, Schalke and FC Nurnberg.

The then 32-year-old had more than 60 caps for his country at that point, and his signing was seen as a coup for Southampton as they looked to achieve instant promotion back to the promised land.

Speaking on the day he signed, Hajto said:

Southampton are a big club. Over the years I have watched a lot of Premier League football and they have always been there and I hope to help them get back there.

"They are among the favourites to go up and they have a lot of ambition to do that. They had 27 years at that level and deserve to be there."

Strangely, despite being a central defender, Hajto was handed the number seven shirt by the club, which had famously been worn by Matthew Le Tissier, one of the greatest Premier League players of all time, just a few years before.

While he was a centre-back by trade, Hajto was actually often used as a right-back in the early months of his Saints career, having been viewed as a back-up option by Redknapp in the middle.

The early indications were promising as Hajto showed that as well as being an assured defender, he was also comfortable on the ball too, as he liked to produce crossfield passes to his teammates.

He began to be left out of the squad before Redknapp left the club in December, and his replacement George Burley agreed to cancel his contract in January to allow him to join Derby County instead.

Hajto signed an 18-month deal with the Rams, but lasted just four months and five appearances before his contract was again terminated early, and he returned to Poland having failed to make his stamp on English football.

Less than a year later, Hajto killed a female at a pedestrian crossing in Lodz in February 2007 while speeding, and in January 2008 he was subsequently found guilty of manslaughter.

After pleading guilty to the charges, the then 34-year-old was given a suspended two-year jail sentence, valid for four years, as he avoided actually going to prison.

Hajto was also ordered to pay 7,000 zloty, and was given a one-year driving ban, and his punishment allowed him to take the step towards management.

He went on to manage LUKS Gomunic, Jagiellonia Bialystok and GKS Tychy in his homeland, with little success.

Hajto hit the headlines again in 2023 when he criticised Aston Villa defender Matty Cash for leaving international duty early, with the right-back posting on X that he was 'talking absolute s***'.

#1336. RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Protection against the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) must expand to lower-income countries, which are harder hit.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

“Something’s wrong with the data. There are too few people in hospitals” with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), epidemiologist Caroline Klint Johannesen recalls a colleague remarking while analysing Danish health records for last winter.

On 1 October 2025, Denmark introduced a nationwide policy of vaccinating pregnant people against RSV — a respiratory pathogen that usually causes mild symptoms but can lead to severe disease and even death in vulnerable people, including infants and older adults. Maternal antibodies induced by the vaccine cross the placenta to protect babies for around the first six months of their lives, when they are most at risk. Newborns at high risk of severe disease, including premature infants, whose mothers had not been vaccinated, were given injections of monoclonal antibodies.

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

Johannesen, a vaccine researcher at Nordsjællands Hospital in Hillerød, Denmark, found1 that infant hospital admissions plummeted. The immunizations are working, she says (see ‘Newborn protection’).

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that every year, RSV hospitalizes roughly 3.6 million and kills about 100,000 children under 5 years old. Of these deaths, 97% occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The virus is also dangerous to older adults — although those risks are widely underappreciated by both physicians and the public. Historically, testing has been sparse, and there are no global statistics for RSV-related adult deaths. But over the age of 60, hospitalizations and mortality increase with age, especially in people with other diseases such as chronic heart and lung conditions. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that between around 10,000 and 25,000 people have died in each of the past two winters, especially in older age groups.

Since 2022, when European regulators approved nirsevimab — a long-acting monoclonal antibody against RSV — a second antibody and three vaccines have been developed for use in adults, one of which is suitable for pregnant people.

“It’s just remarkable,” says Buddy Creech, a paediatrician at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, to have gone “from no mechanism to prevent RSV to an embarrassment of riches”. Dozens of countries across Europe, Asia and North and South America have launched various immunization programmes.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03573-3

#1334. Ex-Spurs Captain Called Man Utd Boss Mauricio Pochettino 'Two-Faced’

Exciting times are ahead for Manchester United, as the English giants are about to embark on a new era. Only time will tell if Mauricio Pochettino's spell at Old Trafford goes better than those who have held the job over the past 13 years.

The Argentine takes over from Michael Carrick, who took over from Ruben Amorim, who took over from Erik ten Hag, who took over from Ralf Rangnick, who took over from Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who took over from Jose Mourinho, who took over from Louis van Gaal, who took over from David Moyes.

All of them failed to live up to the lofty standards set by the legendary Sir Alex Ferguson, who departed in 2013 with 13 Premier League titles under his belt. But Pochettino arrives with good pedigree. He knows the Premier League well, having previously coached Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea, and has dealt with other high-pressure jobs, taking charge of Paris Saint-Germain and, most recently, the 2026 World Cup hosts, the United States.

The 54-year-old will aim to change the culture at Old Trafford, and may have to make some unpopular decisions along the way. As a top-level coach, however, he's no stranger to clashing with senior stars.

The Special One made his comments while he was at Manchester United himself.

Upon Pochettino’s arrival at Spurs from Southampton in 2014, he allowed the players to vote on who should wear the armband following the departure of Michael Dawson. The squad picked Younes Kaboul.

Unfortunately, this didn't pan out well for player or coach. Indeed, the centre-back would be sold the following summer, having played just 15 times under Pochettino. His relationship with the Argentine had crumbled to the point where the pair were no longer talking to each other.

In 2016, he accused the then-Tottenham manager of 'disrespecting him.' The Frenchman angrily said:

"The end was not OK [at Tottenham], because the manager disrespected me, 100 percent. When Mauricio first came we had a very nice, human, man-to-man kind of respect. And then something happened and I don't know what it was."

He continued: "I got injured and then he didn't talk to me anymore. Then he was not putting me in the squad for no reason. One game, two games, three games, and that was strange for me because I am supposed to be his captain.

"I'm not saying because I'm his captain I need to play, no, no, no. If I am not good enough to play I am not playing. But you have to respect players, to talk to them and explain why they're not playing.

"After a few games I went to see him, to ask what was happening. I needed to understand because clearly he wasn't talking to me. But he said: 'There's nothing, I've got nothing to say to you.'"

He said after getting no clear explanation from the Spurs boss, they soon 'stopped talking to each other.'

The ex-Spurs captain carried a grudge as well. In 2018, Kaboul would reflect on their bad relationship once more. This time, he called Pochettino 'two-faced,' explaining:

"The one where things didn’t go well was Pochettino. On the field, nothing to say, very good manager, with a philosophy and a style of play that works.

"Personally, it’s the opposite. He’s two-faced. He would say things to you and did the complete opposite behind your back.”

“I didn’t like that, and I told him. That’s all."

It will be very interesting to see if Pochettino treats any of his new Man Utd stars in a similarly ruthless fashion. He will certainly need everyone pulling in the right direction if he wants to succeed at Old Trafford.
